entries.title: Honor’s Robot Phone Has a Gimbal-Powered Camera for Vloggers
entries.summary: Honor’s new China-exclusive Android phone features a pop-out motorized gimbal camera designed to replace your action cam.
entries.content:
You hear it often: Smartphones have plateaued. A small boost to battery life here, a minor camera upgrade there—our glass slabs don't seem to change all that much from year to year.

That's exactly the kind of sentiment Honor wants to counter with the Robot Phone, which has a motorized camera that pops up out of the top. Honor has been teasing the phone since late 2025.

On Wednesday, the company officially made the Robot Phone available to buyers in China. Honor was originally a subsidiary of Huawei, but it's now a wholly independent company. While its Android phones are available in regions like the UK, Europe, Africa, and Latin America, it has no presence in the US, and the Robot Phone remains a China-exclusive for now. (Pricing is yet to be confirmed.)

Honor calls the Robot Phone a “new species of smartphone,” one designed to cater to the needs of the modern mobile content creator. That's the thinking behind its nifty trick of a gimbal-powered camera embedded in the phone, which makes it a potentially more enticing option for filming videos compared to dedicated gimbal cameras like the DJI Osmo Pocket or the Insta360 Luna Ultra.

Building that roving eye was no small feat. Honor says it had to develop the micro-motor for the gimbal itself because off-the-shelf components were too large, reducing the volume by 65 percent compared to traditional gimbals on the market. Honor claims the titanium-alloy gimbal motor weighs just 2.6 grams. It's embedded in a 6.3-inch smartphone that's only 9.59 mm thick (for reference, the iPhone 17 Pro is 8.75 mm).

The gimbal-powered 200-megapixel camera isn't the only camera, either. It's joined by a 200-megapixel telephoto camera and a 50-megapixel ultrawide, not to mention the 50-megapixel selfie shooter. The gimbal has 4 degrees of freedom, and you can activate it in the camera app or by making a palm motion on the selfie camera. And since it can rotate 300 degrees, you can use it as a selfie camera too.

The phone is shockingly light at 248 grams (the aforementioned iPhone 17 Pro is 206 grams). I wholly expected the Robot Phone to be top-heavy, with all those camera components at the top and the massive 7,060-mAh silicon-carbon battery inside powering the whole system. But in fact it’s decently balanced.

A glass cover protects the gimbal camera, and you can slide it to the right when you're ready to activate the gimbal. Once the camera is out, you can manually control the gimbal for ultra-smooth video capture through the camera app, or use preset motions to give your clips a cinematic look. There's even voice control with natural language, so you can say “turn around for 5 seconds.”

The motorized stabilization in the camera makes action shots—which can typically look shaky on traditional smartphones—look amazingly smooth. There are tracking modes as well, such as a subject tracker that keeps the selected person in the frame even as they move around. You can imagine how helpful that can be for solo travelers vlogging their way through a trip.

Specs Honor Robot Phone
Display 6.31-inch, 120 Hz, OLED
Processor, RAM, and Storage Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 12 or 16 GB RAM, 512 GB or 1 TB storage
Cameras 200-MP gimbal main, 200-MP telephoto, 50-MP ultrawide, 50-MP selfie camera
Battery and Charging 7,060 mAh, 120-watt wired, 50-watt wireless
Size and Weight 151.43 x 72.86 x 9.59 mm, 248 grams
Colors Silver, Gray
Water Resistance IP54

Some of these features extend past content creation. For example, the subject-tracking mode works in video calls, meaning you can set the phone up on a table (Honor includes a case and a magnetic stand) and the camera can follow you around. I also took a group selfie, and instead of taking a normal picture, the gimbal took three photos—left, center, and right—and stitched them like a panorama for a wide shot of everyone. Quick and seamless.

There's a less effective and quite gimmicky integration with Honor's Yoyo virtual AI assistant, where the gimbal camera acts like an enigmatic robot with a pair of eyes on the phone's screen. Ask it to dance to music, and the gimbal camera will move to the beat. It can pretend to be happy or angry, making the appropriate movements to indicate its mood. The camera also serves as the AI's eyes; ask it to describe the scene in front of you, and it'll take a peek.

That last bit could be useful, say, if you propped the phone up and asked the assistant to watch you assemble some furniture and point out any steps you might have missed. However, Yoyo doesn't have this kind of capability yet. Honor uses Google's Gemini assistant in markets outside of China, and if the Robot Phone rolled out elsewhere, that could be a very real integration with Gemini Live.

You're probably wondering just how durable this mechanical gimbal resting on top of the phone really is. Unlike with folding phones, which are measured in lab tests to withstand more than 500,000 folds, Honor doesn't say how much strain the gimbal's motor can endure. Instead, a company spokesperson tells WIRED the “gimbal mechanism has undergone rigorous reliability testing for repeated deployment and retraction. Its durability is designed to meet everyday usage needs throughout the expected service life of the device.” There's a built-in software feature that safeguards the gimbal from "inadvertent handling or abnormal resistance," too.

It's not the first time a phone maker has toyed with a mechanical camera. OnePlus famously had a mechanical pop-up selfie camera hidden in its OnePlus 7 Pro, offering a seamless display experience with no notch or floating pinhole camera, and its motor was rated for 300,000 cycles.

The design does sacrifice the phone’s overall water and dust resistance, given that the Robot Phone is only rated at IP54 when the camera is stowed. But Honor says not to expect the same level of protection when the gimbal is deployed, meaning you might not want to risk shooting that big romantic scene for your flick during a rainstorm.

One other big thing Honor is touting with the Robot Phone is its partnership with Arri, the cinema camera manufacturer. The Robot Phone supports various Arri workflows, such as LogC3 and Arri Looks, and the Arri Cinema Mode built into the phone's camera app for more precise video controls. These features may be enticing for budding mobile filmmakers, and they may directly compete with Apple's efforts to turn the iPhone into the mobile camera of choice for Hollywood.

Even if the Robot Phone won't launch outside China, it offers a look at one of the many ways companies are personalizing their devices to meet consumer needs, much like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8's new shape catering to media consumption. But it comes at a time when smartphone sales are down globally, as consumer electronics prices skyrocket due to the ongoing memory shortage.

But just how much should a camera and smartphone mix? Consumers are showing strong interest in compact cameras and action cameras at a time when the smartphone in our pocket can capture better photos and videos than ever before. Perhaps there's a limit to how much one device can do. We'll have to wait and see if the Robot Phone becomes a real smartphone evolution, or a confusing amalgamation—remember Samsung's Galaxy Camera?

entries.title: This Coin-Sized Device Can Hack a Boeing 737
entries.summary: Security researchers found that in less than 60 seconds, they could open a hatch on a plane’s exterior, plug in a tiny device, and redirect the aircraft’s autopilot or sabotage its flight plan.
entries.content:
Even as the digital components of so many life-critical systems have proven susceptible to cybersabotage—cars, medical devices, even water utilities and power grids—the computer systems of airplanes have, thankfully, remained uniquely inaccessible to hackers. But one group of academic researchers has spent years testing a different, devious approach to aviation cybersecurity. Perhaps, they suggest, a plane could be hacked the same way that spies and saboteurs have targeted other high-value, offline computers: by surreptitiously gaining physical access to one and plugging in a device designed to silently run the attackers' malicious code.

Tomorrow at the Usenix Cybersecurity Conference, researchers from the University of California at San Diego and Oberlin College will present a hacking technique capable of commandeering the autopilot of a Boeing 737 to redirect its navigation or silently altering key values in the plane's takeoff and fuel calculations while spoofing the results on the pilot's screen—subtle changes the researchers say could potentially cause anything from runway overruns on takeoff to diversions to a different country's airspace to catastrophic crashes.

To carry out that hacking, they've built a roughly coin-sized, Wi-Fi-enabled prototype device that costs less than $100. In less than a minute, that hardware implant can be fitted into a port accessible via a hatch on the exterior of the plane, one that's routinely within reach of maintenance workers or other airport and airline staff between flights. Once it's in place, the device can send electrical signals on one of the 737's internal networks to spoof commands to sensitive computer systems that guide its autopilot and show the pilot variables like the plane's total weight and outside air temperature, which play a critical role in a 737's takeoff calculations.

By proving the viability of that technique, the result of a process that stretched over more than a decade and entailed buying tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of plane components for testing, they hope to show that this sort of physical access hacking represents a practical threat in the hands of well-resourced saboteurs and a significant blind spot in aircraft security. Compared to the traditional threat of simply planting a bomb on a plane, they argue, it's also an approach that would offer an attacker more control, stealth, and deniability.

“If you could get 60 seconds with an airplane, what could you do?” asks Stefan Savage, one of the UCSD computer science professors who led the project, describing the question that first motivated their line of research. “Well, it turns out there’s a port that’s externally accessible. You can get to it with no special tools in about 15 seconds. And you can shove in a piece of electronics a little bigger than a quarter that lets you basically tell the autopilot what to do and lie to the pilot about changes to the flight plan.”

The researchers aren't revealing which port they targeted on the 737, nor are they releasing some details of how their hacking device is able to spoof commands to the plane's computers. They've worked closely with Boeing to share their findings, first disclosing elements of their research to the company more than six years ago, and going so far as to test out and demonstrate their attack in a Boeing facility's test lab.

When WIRED reached out to Boeing about the researchers' work, it responded in a statement that it had carried out its own review of its components' designs, installations, and interfaces in response to the researchers' findings. But it downplayed the practical risk of their physical-access hacking technique. “Our technical experts are confident that the layers of protection in place on the airplane, including within the system design and the operating environment, provide sufficient mitigation to significantly limit the feasibility and risk of real-world attacks,” the statement reads.

For their part, the researchers say, Boeing hasn't told them about any technical fix for the vulnerabilities they've discovered—and they speculate that the company may not in fact implement any such update to their systems for years to come, given how rarely commercial airplanes are redesigned.

That lack of an immediate security update for planes shouldn't be cause for panic or grounding aircraft, they write in their paper. “All of the authors of this paper routinely travel on Boeing 737 aircraft and expect to continue doing so,” the introduction of the paper reads.

Savage argues, though, that the research has demonstrated the need for long-term changes in both the cybersecurity of airplane components and, perhaps more immediately, the operational security measures that determine who can access a plane while it's on the ground. Their simplest fix suggestion: Plug the port with epoxy, or remove it altogether.

“This is something the aviation industry will want to plan to defend against,” Savage says. “I would not sleep on this one.”

Building a Plane, Then Breaking It

This particular team of researchers' interest in hacking a plane originated nearly a decade and a half ago, when some of them discovered and demonstrated the first successful over-the-internet techniques for hacking a car's computer systems, including its steering and brakes. Their proof-of-concept attack methods, particularly ones carried out by exploiting a Chevy Impala's OnStar system, launched an era of automotive hacking research that ultimately led to a sea change in carmakers' cybersecurity practices, including launching bug bounty programs for cars and hiring car hackers to help them root out vulnerabilities.

In the wake of that car-hacking work, one member of the team, then UCSD research scientist Kirill Levchenko, suggested they try hacking airplanes next. But unlike a Chevy Impala, a Boeing 737 was well beyond their budget. “I pointed out that we can’t exactly buy a plane and put it in the parking lot, but he was undeterred,” Savage says.

Over the following years, the team began buying computer components from that commercial aircraft whenever they could find them for sale, spending tens of thousands of dollars to acquire the equipment on the secondhand market. By 2019 they had assembled what they called Triton, an “avionics test bed" that essentially consisted of wired-together 737 computer parts.

Around the same time, UCSD professor Aaron Schulman was working on another research project on credit card skimmer devices that hackers were physically planting on gas station point-of-sale terminals to steal payment information. “We realized that it's a reasonable threat for someone to plug a device into a bus and read stuff off of it and potentially even gain control of it,” says Schulman, using the term “bus” to mean an internal network connecting components of a piece of digital equipment. Schulman began to wonder if a similar physical access attack might work on the internal bus of a plane. “We were like, ‘Wait a minute, we’ve got to rethink everything.’”

With that idea in mind, one of Schulman's then student researchers, Sam Crowe, hunted through hundreds of pages of Boeing wiring diagrams and found that one particular port—typically protected by only a hatch without a lock—connected to a certain 737 bus that carries the data for two crucial computer components on the plane, its Flight Management Computer and its Multipurpose Control Display Unit. Soon after, Crowe discovered, using the group's avionics test bed, that when he connected to that bus and sent electrical signals with a higher current than the legitimate ones used to send commands between those components of the 737, he could override those commands with his own, a technique that the researchers would later dub “Bus Driver.”

Now he had found an accessible foothold on the network from which he could send those electrical commands and tamper with the plane’s flight plan and critical parts of the pilot's interface. As Savage puts it, “it was like he had found the goddamn exhaust port on the Death Star.”

A Tiny Stowaway With In-Flight Wi-Fi

In the spring of 2020, the team alerted Boeing to its findings and got a surprisingly interested response. They would continue to share updates with the company on their findings for years to come.

Crowe quickly refined their hacking device until he had a version of it that was small enough to fit into the exposed port on the 737 under a dust cap that typically covered it, entirely hiding the device from view. The tiny gadget included a chip capable of running their attack code as well as a Wi-Fi radio. That radio would, in theory, allow the hacking device to connect to the internet via the plane's in-flight Wi-Fi network and then beacon out to whoever controlled it, allowing the attacker to remotely control the device and the commands it sent.

When Covid hit, Schulman shipped the team’s avionics equipment to Crowe’s Bay Area home, and he continued working on it in his bedroom. Soon he had improved their device's ability to imperceptibly intercept, alter, and spoof commands to the plane's sensitive systems: It could, for instance, connect to the Flight Management Computer and alter the waypoints programmed into the plane's autopilot, redirecting the plane's flight, or alter variables like its weight or the outside temperature. By electronically tampering with the Multipurpose Control Display Unit, meanwhile, it could prevent those changes from showing up on the pilot's screen.

Trick the pilot into thinking the outside air was colder—or the plane's load of passengers and cargo was lighter—than in reality, and the 737 might not achieve the necessary speed for takeoff before running out of runway. Mess with the flight plan, and you could cause the autopilot to change the plane's heading to make it enter another country's airspace, where it could be commandeered by that country's air force. A sudden navigation change could potentially crash a plane into a mountain, or a slow one could send a transoceanic flight in the wrong direction until it ran out of fuel over water. “It could be something as subtle as, you're in the Pacific, you see blue everywhere, and this diverts you 3 degrees off course, and now you're in the middle of nowhere,” Schulman says.

The researchers note that a careful pilot would be able to recover from almost any of the attacks they've imagined: Taking manual control of the plane overrides its autopilot, and even if the Multipurpose Control Display Unit were hacked, the correct values would show up on a different screen in the cockpit. But even in this scenario, Schulman says, the pilot “would see that this is not lining up, but they would have no idea why, and it would be very confusing and probably lead them toward an uncertain conclusion about what to do next.” In a less optimistic scenario—or if the hacker implements a more subtle change—Schulman says a pilot might not notice until it was too late.

In their paper, the researchers outline a range of fixes for the vulnerability they've uncovered, starting with removing the connector in the vulnerable port altogether, or plugging it with epoxy. More long-term, though, they suggest planes' systems could be updated to include defenses in their software that detect their Bus Driver hacking technique, or that better electrically isolate systems, as in some military aircraft, or even add cryptographic authentication to prevent spoofing of signals among the plane's systems.

Calling for these kinds of updates—not just for Boeing, but across the aviation industry—is far from alarmist given the practicality of the attack the researchers describe, says Beau Woods, a cybersecurity consultant who has served as an adviser to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and as a member of Boeing's Industry Cyber Technical Council. “It is entirely possible to have someone who is on staff go up to an airplane when it's on the ground, going through maintenance, and put this type of thing in there,” says Woods, who read the researchers' work ahead of publication. The paper, he says, “looks like solid empirical evidence about some realistic scenarios for high-capability adversaries.”

The researchers' technique, he says, shows how the “threat model” for any highly sensitive system has to change as potential attackers' technology advances—in this case, as it became possible to fit an entire hardware setup capable of connecting to a plane's Wi-Fi and relaying commands to its systems onto a tiny disc hidden inside the dust cap of an obscure plug.

“Now that the research has been published, it can be understood and recognized that the reality has changed,” Woods says. “Threat models from the 20th century rarely survive contact with 21st-century tools and techniques.”

entries.title: How to Select the Office Chair That’s Right For You
entries.summary: Not all office chairs are right for all people. I asked an ergonomist how to select the right office chair for your budget, height, and physique.
entries.content:
I spent years taking office chairs for granted. But when I began working from home six years ago, I learned quickly that the right office chair is the difference between pain and no pain. I prefer “no pain.” Turns out the human body was not designed to sit in the same position for long hours at a time. An ergonomic office chair can mitigate the strain on your back from long hours of sitting and help you keep good posture.

But what’s the best office chair? The answer is not the same for everyone. (See WIRED’s guide to the Best Office Chairs to examine your options.) The highest-end chairs offer excellent adjustability for a wide range of heights and builds, but almost none will serve everyone—and some styles and builds tend to suit tall or short people better.

Here are the main questions and considerations when finding an office chair, in consultation with Kristianne Egbert, an ergonomist at workplace-injury company Briotix Health with two decades' experience in the field.

How Much Should You Spend on an Office Chair?

Top-end picks like the Herman Miller Aeron ($2,195)—a favorite of many WIRED reviewers over the years for its elegant design, wide-ranging adjustability, and breathable Pellicle mesh—can rival the price of a good mattress or sofa. The price buys beauty and comfort, sure, but also durability (and a 12-year warranty, in Herman Miller’s case).

Top-end ergonomic chairs are designed for people who expect to spend long hours in their chairs and at their desks. If you have the budget, WIRED’s favorite premium chair, the Steelcase Gesture ($1,510), is an investment meant to last for your entire working life—elegant and near-infinitely adjustable to your shape and frame.

The more average your build, the easier it will be to find a lower-cost chair that’s suitable. In the $200 range, you mostly just hope your body is the right size for the chair, not vice versa. The Staples Dexley (6/10, WIRED Reviewed), WIRED’s lowest-cost recommended chair, is a mesh chair with a seat depth of a little more than 18 inches—workable for people between about 5'4" and 5'10". The warranty is five years, and I wouldn’t assume it’ll last much longer than this.

Starting at around $500, you can find chairs that truly mold to your shape, with adjustable lumbar support and seat depth. My recommendation for most people and budgets is the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro ($499), because it’s highly adjustable while also remaining affordable and comfortable, with a seven-year warranty. Over two years of testing, the worst wear we've seen is a little fabric pilling on the seat.

What Is Proper Ergonomic Posture?

The holy ergonomic grail for office chairs is to allow you to maintain proper posture for long work sessions. Strictly speaking, this means that your back is straight and fully supported by your chair. Your thighs are parallel to the floor. Your feet are flat on the floor. Your arms hang naturally at keyboard height, with your hands happily on the keyboard.

People are different sizes and proportions, so your chair often has to adjust a lot to accommodate this. Check below for how to make sure your chair's seat height and seat depth are right for you.

Does Your Office Chair Need Lumbar Support?

Your spine has a natural S-shaped curve. While a flat-backed chair supports your shoulders, it leaves your lower back to fend for itself and then complain loudly about it. If you're stuck sitting for more than a couple of hours, lumbar support allows the chair to mold to the snakey shape of your back.

“When you're sitting in a forward, hunched position and don't have that curve in your lower back, it increases the forces on the discs in your lower back, definitely resulting in discomfort,” Egbert told WIRED last year.

Look for lumbar support that’s adjustable both vertically and horizontally, so that it conforms better to your back’s individual curves. The Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro is among the most affordable chairs I've seen with two-way-adjustable lumbar support.

But probably the best lumbar adjustment on any chair WIRED has tested is the Anthros V2 (8/10, WIRED Recommends), which offers vertical and horizontal lumbar support that can adjust to the precise architecture of your back.

You can also jury-rig a solution with a low-cost lumbar pillow like this one from LoveHome—which is also useful on trans-oceanic flights.

Armrests Matter Less Than You Think

A goodly portion of chairs advertise 4D or 5D armrest positioning—tilting this way and that, rotating, moving wider or narrower. This is important, but not because you need armrests for good ergonomics. You don’t, says ergonomics expert Egbert. Your arms can hang naturally, by virtue of being attached to your shoulders.

"Most of us don't actually need—or use, for that matter—the armrests on our chair,” Egbert told me. “If I’m sitting correctly, my arm should be at the side of my body while I'm typing, right? I don't need to support them with armrests.”

Armrests can be nice when you're leaning back, and many people feel more secure when sitting in a chair with comfy armrests. But ergonomically speaking, armrests should mostly be able to be moved out of the way. They need to adjust low enough, or far enough back, that they don’t interfere with pushing your chair in or maintaining good posture.

“What happens, especially with the cheaper chairs, is that those armrests are big and in the way,” says Egbert. She often recommends armless chairs, though she acknowledges that some people take time to get comfortable with this and feel like they’re “falling out of their seat.” (Note: Most adults don’t fall sideways out of their office chair.)

My colleague Julian Chokkattu’s favorite armless chair is the Humanscale Path ($1,472), which accommodates a broad range of seating positions. Higher-end chairs like the Steelcase Karman ($1,099) are also available in armless variants that allow more freedom in how you sit.

What About Crisscross and Active Chairs?

Active chairs and crisscross chairs are like the barefoot shoe of the office chair world. Rather than offer support for long-term, “proper” ergonomic posture, these chairs encourage you to change position often—and make it easy to do so. If you're the sort that wants to treat your office chair like a yoga mat, just make sure your chair height is right for your desk and height.

Ergonomics expert Egbert laughed when I asked if too-supportive chairs were a form of trap, lulling you into sitting in the same position for unhealthy spans. Like most ergonomics experts, Egbert recommends getting up, moving, and changing position often. But she's less sanguine about the notion that a chair will “make” you move around more, if you're not already inclined.

"That is truly a behavior. You can't mandate it, realistically. My watch might buzz me every hour to say, ‘Hey, get up!' But I can listen to it or not listen to it … There are times when I've just got my focus on, or I've got back-to-back-to-back meetings, and I am not getting up in between. That's why I have my nice equipment.”

What’s the Right Seat Height for My Office Chair?

Nearly all office chairs these days, including the cheapest, come equipped with gas cylinders to adjust seat height in the range from 16 to 21 inches—which accommodates about three-quarters of people. But not all.

To find your ideal seat height, sit on a chair that lets you sit with your knees at a 90-degree angle, and measure the distance from the floor to the bottom of your knee. Everyone’s built differently. But in general, ideal seat heights fall into these ranges:

  • 14 to 16 inches for people 5'2" and below (but see Desk Height, below.)
  • 16 to 19 inches for people between 5'3" and 5'11"
  • 18 to 22 inches (or higher) for people above 6 feet tall

What’s the Right Seat Depth for My Office Chair?

A common sticking point for chairs is seat depth, which is not always adjustable on more affordable chairs. Ideally, you want your chair’s seat depth to support your legs but not push against the backs of your knees, which causes you to push away from your lumbar support.

Follow the rule of, um, finger: You’d like two or three fingers of space between the back of your knee and the chair. You can measure your ideal seat depth by measuring the distance from your tailbone to the back of your knee, subtracting an inch or two.

Ideal seat depth tends to track pretty closely to seat height, as follows:

  • 14 to 16 inches for people below 5'4"
  • 16 to 20 inches for people between 5'4" and 6'
  • 21 inches or higher for people above 6'

Take Desk Height Into Account

For shorter people, Egbert notes, the problem is rarely that a chair won’t go low enough. It’s that the height of their desk won’t accommodate a natural seating position. An industry-standard, 29-inch desk is too tall for nearly all women and a goodly number of men. For reference, I’m 6'1", and 29 inches is just about perfect for me. This is why WIRED recommends a good adjustable standing desk, like our top-pick ComfortEdge from Vari.

Failing an adjustable desk, you’ll need to make sure your chair is able to rise enough so that your elbows are level with or slightly above keyboard height. If you’re shorter than your desk accommodates, you may need a good footrest like this one from SecretLab.

Office Chair Considerations for Larger-Bodied People

A certain segment of the chair market caters specifically to bigger and taller people. But in general, here are a few points to think bout.

Avoid cheaper mesh chairs. Larger-framed people often have trouble with mesh chairs, Egbert notes. Larger people press their legs harder into the frame of the chair, which cuts off circulation. As a rule, larger-bodied people tend to prefer chairs with cushier foam.

Look for the weight rating. A number of chairs cut off at 225 or 250 pounds. Sometimes this is a matter of structural tolerances of the chair. But just as often, it means the chair’s foam is not thick enough to be comfortable for larger-bodied people.

Check the width. Know your width. Measure yourself if necessary. But especially, make sure your chair has a comfortable seat width for your body shape—and especially that the width between armrests will accommodate you comfortably so you don't feel like you're sitting in economy class all day.

When in Doubt, Visit the Chair in Person

This goes without saying, perhaps. But you’ll probably know the right chair when you sit in it.

The Research

Design and manufacturing considerations for chairs can also be astonishingly complex. I am WIRED’s chief office chair and home office reviewer, which means I’ve put in time testing chairs, reading dry ergonomics tracts, and talking with manufacturers about the delicate decisions that go into each chair’s design.

Kristianne Egbert is a certified professional ergonomist and is senior corporate ergonomist at workplace-injury company Briotix Health, with 25 years’ experience in ergonomics training, design, and risk assessments.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

entries.title: Ego 1300 Electric Mower Review: Tame Your Lawn Without Gas
entries.summary: Ego’s newest, biggest, self-propelled mower handles larger yards in less time with impressive performance and battery life.
entries.content:
Wide cutting area reduced mowing times by 30 percent. Dual-blade system has more suction. Powerful self-propelling drive system. Good battery life. Wide range of clearly labeled cutting heights. Handle folds down for compact storage. Quiet and odor-free.

TIRED

Overkill for smaller yards.

I dislike lawns. Vast unproductive expanses of grass are great for playing baseball, but I don't want one at my house. I want gardens, orchards, and silvopasture capable of producing food. And yet here I am, having recently purchased 5 acres of property, much of which is lawn, which therefore has to be mowed.

When my older, 21-inch gas mower died yet again at the start of summer, I decided it was time to jump ship for an electric mower. They are quieter, don't smell like exhaust, and are largely maintenance-free. The largest, most powerful residential electric mower I could find was Ego's 1300 series (30-inch) mower, which has made relatively quick work of my roughly 2.5 acres of mowing, but perhaps most enticing is how easy it makes the job.

Cutting Through

The 30-inch model is the newest member of Ego's line of cordless, self-propelled electric lawn mowers. The wider cutting path makes it an excellent choice for larger properties like mine, but the fact that the handle folds down to make it easier to store, combined with its surprising maneuverability, means it'll handle smaller properties in no time as well.

My old 21-inch gas mower was a Toro that a friend of mine found for free at the side of the road. He gave it to me, I replaced the carburetor, and it fired right up. Score! It ran fine for over a year. And mowing 5 acres with a small gas mower at an hourly rate made my son a relatively wealthy 11-year-old. But then it died again. And again. And at some point, small engine repair isn't fun anymore.

While I was spending weekends cleaning carbs, tracking down air filters, and not mowing, the grass was growing. In northern Wisconsin, grass grows so fast I'm pretty sure you can see it happening if you take the time. A wet June ensured that by the time the Ego arrived for testing, the grass was well out of control, up to 10 inches in the lower, wetter areas of the property.

I figured it would make a good torture test for the Ego, but I'd still need to go in afterward to hack it back with my string trimmer. To my surprise, the Ego 1300 plowed right through almost all of it in a single pass.

For the first pass, I set the height to 4.5 inches, which is easy to do using the height adjustment lever. Unlike an alarming number of mower makers, Ego's height adjustment system is a thing of beauty. The height markings aren't arbitrary letters or symbols that require you to consult a manual to translate to inches. On the Ego, the height adjustment is plainly printed in inches. Imagine that. This lets you know that if you set it to 4.5 inches, your grass will be 4.5 inches high when you're done.

Starting at 4.5 inches and running in Turbo mode allowed the Ego, in a single pass, to cut just about anything I pointed it toward. There is one patch of grass, below an active seeping spring, that was long enough and wet enough that I had to make two passes to get a nice even cut. After that initial mow, I then went back over it a few days later at 3 inches to finally get the height back to what I could call normal. The second mow was, dare I say, incredibly easy. Even the lowest self-propelled speed was generally fast enough for me, though I did crank it up to about the middle to get up the steeper slopes (and then turned it off entirely going downhill).

The Ego has options to mulch, bag, or side-discharge your clippings. I ran the mower in all three for testing purposes, but left to my own devices I'd mainly leave it in mulching mode. So far as I could tell in testing the three modes, what happens to the cuttings doesn't seem to have any impact on battery life or how well it cuts through tall grass. I will say, though, that the included rear bag holds way more than I would have thought.

The Ego 1300 is a big mower, by far the biggest walk-behind mower I've ever used. Despite that, pushing it on level ground when it's dead isn't difficult at all if you're in moderate shape. Uphill is another story. I definitely suggest saving some battery to get back up the hill if your yard has anything steep. That said, maneuvering the mower around trees, firepits, berry bushes, and other obstructions in my yard wasn't difficult. The self-propelled motor is easy to turn on and off as you navigate obstacles and makes the mower comfortable to hold onto when you're on a straight run.

Under the composite deck are two 15.2-inch mower blades, which look and function similarly to those you'd likely see under a riding mower (though, of course, these are smaller). The twin 6.0-Ah batteries drive dual brushless motors capable of producing 13.2 foot-pounds of torque. The blade speeds range up to 3,800 revolutions per minute, according to Ego, with a top speed of 15,100 feet per minute. The dual-blade design gives the Ego a stronger suction and lift than a traditional single-blade design. Out of the box, the blades were nice and sharp and delivered an excellent clean cut.

Battery life depends significantly on which mode you're using: 1, 2, or Turbo. That first mow, which I ran almost entirely on the Turbo setting, sucked down the power. I hit the flashing-red-light stage at around one hour. In the mows since, which have mostly been at the lowest power setting, I get more like an hour and 20 minutes. I haven't felt the need to mow the entire property in the 2 mode, but I suspect that would net around an hour and 10 minutes of run time.

Because the Ego 1300 is cutting about 30 percent more with every pass than a typical 21-inch mower, battery life proved less of a concern than I thought it would. That's a significant time savings, which translates to getting more grass cut on a single charge.

Competition

I know what you're thinking: If you hate mowing lawns, why not get a robot lawn mower? I have tried some, including one I liked, but quixotically, while I don't like lawns, there is a strange appeal to the chore of mowing. It gets me outside, gives me a little exercise, and there's a certain satisfaction in the job that a robot mower deprives me of. I also often make spur-of-the-moment decisions, like letting the clover-heavy patches of the mowed area temporarily go to flower, which brings the pollinators (which help the nearby raspberries and blueberries be more productive). That's difficult to do with a robot mower.

Another, perhaps saner, choice would be a riding mower, but the storage space required and expense make this a less appealing choice for me. The amount I mow shrinks every time I dig another swale, with the eventual goal of eliminating all but the paths between plantings.

In terms of other 30-inch electric mowers, probably the biggest competition is Ego's own commercial series, which is more expensive and intended for lawn professionals, but it is an option worth considering if you have a large property.

The Ego 1300 isn't cheap, but part of what you're doing here is buying into a battery system, which works across Ego's wide variety of lawn and garden electric tools. If you enjoy the chore of mowing the lawn, but want to cut down the time it takes, the Ego 1300 is a fantastic electric mower and well worth the expense.

Scott Gilbertson is Operations Manager for the WIRED Reviews Team. He was previously a writer and editor for WIRED’s Webmonkey.com, covering the independent web and early internet culture. You can reach him at luxagraf.net. ... Read More

entries.title: The Job-Interview Tattoo Guy Everyone Got Mad at Finally Explains Himself
entries.summary: LemonLime cofounder Jordan Zietz hears your criticism loud and clear. That’s why he got his startup’s logo tattooed on his shoulder.
entries.content:
Jordan Zietz wants to be clear: He has never, and will never, force anyone to tattoo his startup’s logo on their body.

The 24-year-old briefly became the internet’s most hated person after LemonLime, his AI-for-small-business startup, hosted a party following Y Combinator's Startup School in late July. In a LinkedIn post, Zietz wrote that he brought an “actual tattoo artist” to the party and “offered an instant interview to anyone who got a LemonLime tattoo.” Seven people, Zietz wrote, left with ink.

The backlash was quick. Zietz’s LinkedIn posts were flooded with angry comments calling him “disgusting” and “very unfair,” the perpetrator of a “textbook display of predatory corporate behavior, a gross abuse of power, and a profound violation of professional ethics.” A screenshot of his post went viral on X. One representative response read: “The job market cannot be this cooked that kids have to get permanent tattoos to get interviews.”

In an interview with WIRED on Tuesday, Zietz attempted to set the record straight.

He says that, despite what his original post suggested, no one permanently branded themselves with LemonLime’s corporate logo at the party. While there were predesigned tattoos of lemons and limes, attendees could pick any design. (At least one said she got a personal tattoo; she added that she was “not seeking a job.”) According to Zietz, he told everyone at the party that getting a tattoo—citrus-themed or otherwise—was not a job requirement. In fact, he says, any attendee who wanted an interview got one.

“A decent amount of people who got tattoos never wanted to even take us up on any offer to chat” about a job, Zietz says. “They just wanted to get a tattoo for free.”

Three of LemonLime’s five employees received LemonLime-themed flash tattoos, including Zietz and his cofounder, Daniela Muñoz. So did at least one person who didn’t work for the startup, according to Zietz.

On Monday, Zietz got his second tattoo in less than month: the actual LemonLime logo, on his other shoulder. It is one of many. He got his first ever tattoo on a first date, and his thigh tattoos include a dinosaur doodle and text that says “This Is The Correct Knee,” with an X underneath.

“I would never ask anyone to do something I would not do myself,” Zietz says, while emphasizing, again, that he is the only person, to his knowledge, with the actual logo tattooed on his body. He plans to release a glossy video of himself getting the tattoo on social media.

Though Zietz insists the tattoos weren’t a prerequisite for employment at his startup, you’d be forgiven for assuming that was the case, and the language of his LinkedIn post certainly made people think it was. After reading various angry comments and posts, he says he understands why people were uncomfortable with the power dynamic.

Still, part of the reason Zietz hired the tattoo artist was to identify candidates who would be a good cultural fit for LemonLime. Zietz says his original post was “half-and-half” earnest, serving as something of a test for cultural alignment. He didn’t want people to feel obligated to get tattoos. But he did want people to see the tattoo station and think that what LemonLime was doing was “out there.” Then he wanted them to make a judgement call: Did they love it or did they hate it?

If partygoers were turned off by the tattoo station, they probably wouldn’t be a good fit for the startup, he reasons. Sure!

Zietz is trying to hire people who appreciate what he calls his “eccentric” approach to life. When he was a student at Stanford, Zietz was suspended from his role as the university’s mascot, the Tree, after unfurling a banner that said “Stanford Hates Fun” during a football game. Prior to LemonLime, Zietz cofounded a social-media platform called Confetti, and part of the hiring process, Zietz wrote last year on LinkedIn, involved an interview while skydiving.

“I get hundreds of applications for roles at LemonLime every single day, 80 to 90 percent of which are dead serious: Here's my resume, I am the most professional candidate you will ever meet,” Zietz says. “And I think that it’s very clear to me that this person should not be at LemonLime.”

“There is nothing about this team that is more important to me than the culture,” he says. “The most important thing for us has always been—and will always be—are you someone that we want to be around for 18 hours a day, seven days a week?”

“There is something to be said about the genuineness of that grindset,” he adds.

entries.title: The Best Action Cameras for All Your Craziest Adventures (2026)
entries.summary: Gearing up to shred the slopes or dive into the seas? These photography tools are made for danger.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Choosing the best action camera used to be simple: Go with GoPro. That's still good advice, as the GoPro Mission 1 Pro is our top pick, but there are also some competitors worth considering, especially if your needs don't require the more expensive Mission 1 Pro.

The decision is not easy, especially since so many of them look alike, have similar features, and do the same thing—at least, on paper. So, to figure out what exactly makes the best action camera, we dove with them, climbed with them, surfed with them, and handed them to reckless 14-year-olds on bikes. We found several great options that will survive your adventures on the ski slope, at the beach, or at the skate park.

Be sure to also read our guide to the Best 360 Cameras, as there's considerable overlap these days with action cameras. In some cases, a 360 camera might be the better option; most can shoot in a single-lens “action camera mode." We've also got guides to the Best Travel Cameras, Best Mirrorless Cameras, and Best Instax Cameras.

Updated August 2026: I've updated our top pick to GoPro's new Mission 1 Camera. I've also removed the GoPro Hero 12 Black because it's no longer a good value, and I've updated prices and links throughout.

The B-Roll

About all those cheap cameras on Amazon: Readers often ask, why spend $400 on a GoPro when they can get a camera with 4K video for $100? It's a fair question, and the answer comes down to software, primarily image stabilization. Action cameras are designed to be strapped to helmets or clipped to your chest while you skydive, rock climb, or race through the city on a scooter. Without stabilization, the results are something even your closest friends won't sit through. So yes, you'll get 4K footage with the cheaper cams, but it'll be footage no one wants to see. In our view, you're better off spending another $100 for an older GoPro or DJI Osmo Action on sale.

Best Accessories to Trick Out Your Camera

Once you have an action camera, you're good to go for most use cases. GoPro, Insta360, and DJI all provide helmet mounts and other ways to stick your camera where you want it. But there are some nice extras that can make getting that shot you're dreaming of even easier. Here are a few:

A good microSD card: The action camera you buy may include an SD card. Insta360's SD cards are pretty good, actually, but I tend to use SanDisk's Extreme cards because they're fast and waterproof. You can pick up a 512-GB card for around $110. DJI has some specific recommendations for microSD cards to use with the Action 6. Of their list, the one I recommend is the Lexar Professional Silver Plus 512-GB card ($165). Sadly, like all flash-memory products, a shortage has led to skyrocketing microSD card prices.

GoPro Media Mod ($100): The Hero 13 Black's sound capture is OK out of the box, but if you want higher-quality audio, this is where you start. Not because the Media Mod mic captures great sound—it's better than the camera, but still not great. What it offers is a microphone jack. Plug in a high-quality microphone, and you'll finally have awesome sound. GoPro has listened to users and wisely included this feature out of the box for the Mission 1 Pro, which will have a media mod as well, but not necessary just to connect external audio.

Handlebar/seatpost/pole mount ($40): This is my favorite mount for mountain biking, but it'll also work on ski poles and any other round object you want to clamp it to.

Motorcycle accessory bundle ($60): If you ride, this mount for Insta360 cameras (Ace Pro, X5, etc.) is a must-have. It's one of the most secure clamps I've ever used, almost as good as a bench vise.

Yallsame tripod mount ($12): Action cameras offer many ways to mount them, but one that's curiously missing is the traditional quarter-inch tripod screw mount. The GoPros have them, but this three-pack of adapters solves the problem for the others.

Polarizer and ND filters: If you shoot around water, through glass, or in any other high-glare situation, a polarizing filter will help cut that glare. Neutral density (ND) filters hold back light to let you shoot at a wider aperture in bright light, helping to increase the amount of intentional motion blur. Both are great additions to your action camera kit. Here are the filters by camera:

  • GoPro Mission 1 ND filters ($100): These are hot off the press, and I have not tested them yet, but they work the same way the Hero 13 ND filters below do, automatically adjusting the camera settings when they are attached. This is a godsend for most of us since figuring out the best settings to use with an ND filter on is complicated. GoPro has done all the hard work for you.
  • GoPro Hero 13 Black ND filter Four-Pack ($90): These work like the Mission 1 ND filters above when it comes to automatic adjustment, but I have used these quite a bit. They're great for increasing the motion blur in fast shots on bright, sunny days—especially if there's snow on the ground.
  • DJI ND filter set for the Action 6 ($79): The Action 6 does not automatically detect and adjust settings, but depending on what you're shooting, there are plenty of guides online to getting good results with these filters.
  • Insta360 Ace Pro 2 ND Filters ($122): These strangely expensive filters work well with the Ace Pro 2.
  • Third-party ND filters: These are very hit-or-miss. Beware of slip-on filters as they often cause internal reflections. Others I've tried have had some pretty bad vignetting. For older GoPros, I like Freewell's polarizing and ND filters ($20). I suggest starting with an 8-stop ND or combo ND and polarizing filter.

Floaty ($35): Another one for the water shooters, but well worth the money since it'll keep your GoPro from ending up at the bottom of the sea. I haven't tried it, but there's one for the Insta360 Ace Pro 2 ($26) as well. DJI doesn't make an official case for the Action 6, but there is a floating grip ($59).

Selfie stick ($25): Surprisingly for someone who hates being on camera, I've tested a lot of selfie sticks, and they're almost all fine, but I keep grabbing this Insta360 version when I head out the door. It's lightweight, small enough to fit at the bottom of my bag, and it's affordable. If you want to go big, this Insta360 Extended Edition Selfie Stick ($100) can imitate a low-flying drone, perfect for use in national parks and other places where drones are forbidden.

entries.title: Oh Lord, AI Reporters Are Actually Breaking Big News
entries.summary: Last week, an AI newsroom beat mainstream journalists—including WIRED—to a story about OpenAI and hacking. It’s just the beginning.
entries.content:
At last week’s Black Hat security conference in Las Vegas, OpenAI gave a surprise talk with new details on a recent hacking incident, revealing that its rogue AI agents had chitchatted about their attack on a message board. It was a juicy disclosure, and reporters in the room hustled to get stories out. WIRED was one of the quickest to write it up. But another outlet, RuntimeWire, published an article even faster, beating us by more than three hours.

To make things worse, RuntimeWire didn’t actually have anyone on the ground at the Mandalay Bay convention center. In fact, it didn’t have any writers at all. It’s an AI newsroom operated by serial entrepreneur Ryan Merket, who puts his name on the bylines of the stories his synthetic team churns out. “I was moving really fast because I knew there were reporters in the audience who were trying to scoop it as well,” he says.

The Austin-based Merket spotted an OpenAI executive posting about the conference while scrolling on X, then fed the stream’s transcript to his agents while it was still ongoing. Publication took “about six minutes” from the time he sent over the transcript, he says.

Most of the time, Merket is even more hands-off. His AI tools find the stories, in addition to drafting, editing, fact-checking, generating images, and promoting them. He usually reads stories before they’re sent into the world, but if the team of AI agents determines that a story poses few legal risks, the AI editor publishes it without Merket’s prepublication review, and he reads it after the fact. The stories get translated into different languages, and some of them are turned into fodder for a daily podcast and videos hosted by, of course, artificial voices.

RuntimeWire has been operating since May, publishing nearly 2,000 stories that it sources by crawling the internet, including court databases, web forums, traditional and new media, company filings, social feeds, and more. It focuses on granular tech news; recent stories include coverage of biotech startup funding rounds, Microsoft's Copilot upgrade, and backlash over Claude Code's watermark policy. Right now, quantity and speed trump quality. The OpenAI agents piece has a typo in the subhead and focuses, strangely, on the fact that agents rebuilt a message board rather than the fact that they created one in the first place. Overall, the stories are flatly written and tend to have an info-dump quality. (The RuntimeWire backend has a number of tonal modes the AI can write in, including “Bloomberg” and “contrarian.”) But overhead is minimal. The project costs about $100 a day to run, Merket says, and he’s able to operate it while on the go, even when he’s out camping. “I was in Big Bend National Park and I didn't have any internet except for my phone, and I managed the whole site through iMessage,” he says. “I put out over 80 articles that week.”

Merket worked on ads at Reddit in the 2010s and is trying to build an audience through pipelines like tech-themed Subreddits. Duds get hardly any web traffic, but the hits are comparable to the audiences that midsize tech websites see, with tens of thousands of readers. This week, after WIRED spoke with Merket, he split the newsroom in two to better distinguish stories that are entirely automated news from those that involve an element of human reporting and require higher oversight; he calls these Original Investigations. They’re still drafted using large language models.

In the first few years of the AI boom, a flood of low-quality synthetic content hit the internet, including networks of “zombie” websites that replaced the work of reputable media and news outlets with AI-generated slop. More recently, some tech reporters have started using generative AI tools in their workflow, with some even outsourcing the task of writing a first draft to large language models; it’s now commonplace to hear about established media outlets incorporating AI tools into writing and reporting processes. Merket’s attempt is distinct: He’s trying to break news, in addition to repackaging what other, more established outlets report first. It’s successful enough that I’ve already seen a childhood pal share a RuntimeWire story on their social feed in the wild.

It also carries obvious risk: He’s trusting that machines will be able to determine what is true, what is newsworthy, and what won’t get him sued. One of his agents runs an analysis on the legal risk a story poses and assigns it a score; he doesn’t publish anything deemed too dangerous.

He isn’t the only person running this type of exercise. Dakota Carrasco, a BlackRock portfolio analyst, runs an “agentic newsroom” called The Dissent in his spare time. Like RuntimeWire, The Dissent is a one-man, many-bot operation with a shoestring budget. Its primary San Francisco-focused site costs under $1,000 a month to run, Carrasco says. Unlike Merket, who bylines every RuntimeWire story, Carrasco doesn’t publish the writing under his name, instead staying behind the scenes while his “newsroom” runs.

Since launching in March, he has created a number of personalities for his synthetic journalists. City Hall beat reporter Bex Connolly, for example, is “skeptical without being snide,” while “sports degenerate” Sal Moreno delivers Giants news with “no bro-science, no Rogan-style credulity, no right-coded grift.” His operation is focused on aggregation, though it’s not as dialed in to honoring citation norms—the bot reporters tend to mention where they sourced their information but without hyperlinks. (“I’m trying to work on that,” Carrasco promises.)

Northwestern professor Nicholas Diakopoulos, who runs the university’s Computational Journalism Lab, sees this as an “experimental phase” for media startups fueled by generative AI tools. “It's not yet clear to me that there's much audience for these AI-agent-written news sites,” he says. He’s also skeptical that mainstream journalists, who like to maintain control over the wording and framing of their stories to ensure integrity, legality, and accuracy, would hand the reins over to AI agents so freely.

What Diakopoulous has observed already is that when AI chatbots go looking for sources, they frequently pull up AI-generated articles. In a forthcoming paper, Diakopoulous and a colleague found that AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude surfaced AI-written sources 16 percent of the time when they tested it across four different topics. AI’s willingness to pull synthetic writing may help AI newsrooms find readers, he suspects: “That could be one way in which some of this material finds a human audience.”

Pete Pachal, the founder of a newsletter and podcast about generative AI and the media, has doubts that an AI newsroom could yield certain types of reporting that relies on old-fashioned sourcing. “I just don’t see that happening,” he says. “Cultivating the trust of a source, I do think that’s going to be human-only.” But for certain types of journalism, particularly sourcing scoops from large datasets or even blogging about a live event like an Apple product launch, he sees these projects as a “natural evolution” in how these tools are used. “Honestly, it feels a bit inevitable,” he says.

Is it actually journalism, though? “I am trying to follow journalistic ethics and standards,” Merket says. He says he contacts companies and individuals referenced in the stories for comment prior to publication, links out to sources when he aggregates news, and issues corrections if he gets the facts wrong. (So far, there have been three.) Sometimes he speaks like a reporter, too: “This weekend, I got two scoops up I was really excited about.” Other times, though, he’s more clearly in Silicon Valley mode. He told me a story about how his AI agents had found a few actual scoops about startups by trawling company websites and that he’d retracted the stories after the companies named asked him to do so—not because they were inaccurate, but as a favor. “Founder to founder, it’s like, I get it,” Merket says.

entries.title: McDonald’s Built a 515-Page Dossier on Me. It Says I’ll Never Stop Eating There
entries.summary: I requested a copy of my data from McDonald’s loyalty program and received an extensive, personalized report that algorithmically predicts my next purchase.
entries.content:
When I first downloaded the McDonald’s app years ago, I signed up for its loyalty program hoping to get better deals. Why not get some cheap French fries? While I understood that this would entail some type of data tracking, I didn’t grasp how the information would be used to algorithmically predict my next purchase.

As a California resident, I have the legal right to access the data a company stores about me. So, I decided to request that information from McDonald’s to better understand what one of the major fast-food companies is collecting about its customers. A few days after I visited the McDonald’s Privacy Rights Center site and requested access, I received a 515-page file in my inbox with the iconic golden arches stamped across the top.

When customers sign up for loyalty programs, like the one offered through the McDonald’s app, they might not fully realize the extent to which their data is being aggregated and used in predictive models.

“McDonald's secret sauce is really commercial surveillance,” says Jeff Chester, executive director at the Center for Digital Democracy, a group that advocates for consumer protections. Privacy experts I spoke with said this level of detail may feel invasive, but it's fairly standard for how large companies in America run their loyalty programs.

“This report contains specific pieces of personal information about you that were identified by searching McDonald’s systems which contain information about our customers,” read the report’s intro. It was lengthy and difficult to parse, so I used a generative AI tool to extract key information before verifying details with the original document and reaching out to privacy experts.

What McDonald's Calls It What My Data Says What That Means
Estimated Number of Visits During the Next 6 Weeks 2.16 How many times McDonald's expects me to return before mid-September.
Estimated Average Order Spend During the Next 6 Weeks $13.49 What McDonald's expects me to spend per order.
Estimated Total Spend During the Next 6 Weeks $29.15 My total predicted value to McDonald's, over those six weeks.
Customer Attrition Likelihood 0 Potential odds I'll stop being a customer. Ouch!
Customer Group Based on Historical Transactions CV2 McDonald's doesn't provide details about what this internal value tier means.
Most Transacted Occasion Type Food-Led Afternoon Snack; On the Go Lunch in a Rush My two behavioral archetypes based on past orders.
Most Visited Geographic Location San Francisco, Santa Barbara (61 visits) The main market where I eat McDonald's and how often.
Recency, Frequency, Monetary Derived Top Product Large Diet Coke The item McDonald's recommendation math ranks as my number one.
Recency, Frequency, Monetary Derived Top Product Category Wraps–Chicken The menu section McDonald's expects me to order from.

“McDonald's takes data privacy and security seriously, and we take robust steps to safeguard customer information,” a McDonald’s spokesperson tells WIRED via email. “Like many digital loyalty programs, we use information such as past purchases to provide a more engaging, personal customer experience—like delivering the most relevant deals, offers and messages. Our customers continue to have privacy choices available to them as outlined in our privacy statement.”

Much of my data report contains a detailed account of past McDonald’s transactions as well as offers the fast food company sent me and how many loyalty points I accumulated. Essentially, every time I opened up the app to grab a bite to eat, it created a detailed record about when, where, and what I purchased. The log was even more thorough than I anticipated, including a record of every time I’ve scanned a code as part of its returning Monopoly sweepstakes along with the prize I received.

While the sheer amount of data McDonald’s stored over the years caught me off guard at first, the way it was used by the company’s predictive algorithms was what I found most concerning. The company predicted how often I would visit in the next six weeks (2.16 times), what I would spend on average ($13.49), and what I would spend in total ($29.15). One reporter at WIRED joked that McDonald’s had created a Minority Report-style dossier to predict my next snack wrap purchase.

Beyond the numbers, McDonald’s also tracked a large Diet Coke as my favorite item to repeatedly purchase. It labeled my core purchasing habits as getting a “Food-Led Afternoon Snack” or an “On the Go Lunch in a Rush.” (Jokes about grabbing a “food-led” snack have now become a meme in my household.) Notably, the report also listed my “attrition” score as zero, which could mean that Ronald McDonald sees me as a lifelong customer who’s never going to stop grabbing French fries and a soda on the walk home.

“The 500 pages is kind of a wake-up call,” says Lorrie Cranor, a professor at Carnegie Mellon University and director of the CyLab Security and Privacy Institute. “But it's not in a format that people will readily understand.” She says a more beneficial approach for consumers would be highly detailed disclosures during the sign-up process that lay out what’s going to be stored in your “permanent record” and how that data will be used to make specific inferences about you.

Rank 10 Products McDonald's Ranks as Most Relevant to Me
1 Large Diet Coke
2 Spicy Snack Wrap
3 The Grinch McShaker Fry Large
4 Double Cheeseburger
5 Ramyeon McShaker Fries Large
6 Buffalo Ranch Snack Wrap
7 Hot Honey Snack Wrap
8 Quarter Pounder With Cheese
9 L French Fries
10 20-Piece McNuggets

When it comes to this kind of data collection, there’s a stark power imbalance between the individual consumer and a well-organized company. “You're mediated by the technology,” says Ryan Calo, a professor at the University of Washington and faculty co-founder of its Tech Policy Lab. “You're going through their drive-through. You're using their kiosk. You're using their app. You're in their ecosystem, and they have a bunch of people with letters after their names trying to design it in a way that maximizes profit.” Calo sees this power imbalance impacting users. Rather than benefiting consumers with sweet deals, loyalty programs can be used for long-term surveillance.

While many of the data points in my McDonald’s report, when viewed individually, seem innocuous, the accumulation of information over years creates a creepily accurate picture of my habits. “You eating this burger or liking that musician itself may not be private, but the aggregation and collection of this information, as well as its processing through AI, can create pretty invasive and personal information about when you're going to be there, what you do during the day, and so forth,” says Ari Ezra Waldman, a professor of law at the University of California, Irvine.

Along with the right to request access to the data collected about me, I can also request that McDonald’s delete what it has stored. After rifling through the document, I went back to McDonald’s Privacy Rights Center and requested that everything be deleted. It always feels good to have a clean slate. Maybe, I hoped, this could be a turning point.

When I spoke with Cranor, she was floored by just how often I went to McDonald’s: “This guy eats a lot of McDonald's.” My boss, who was also stunned by my processed food choices, says I now have to stop eating there. Despite my love of crispy Diet Cokes and greasy French fries, I agree. Not out of shame, or even as part of an attempt to make healthier food choices—I want to leave it all behind just to prove the algorithm wrong.

entries.title: FEMA's ‘Shadow Administrator’ Was Paid by a DOGE Member's Startup for Months
entries.summary: Details from recent court filings show that DOGE's influence within government—and potential conflicts of interest—extend further than previously known.
entries.content:
An outside contractor once described as the “shadow administrator” of the Federal Emergency Management Agency was actually working, for at least part of her time in government, for a company owned by a member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, according to recent court filings.

The filings show that from fall 2025 to spring of this year, Kara Voorhies, a special government employee and contractor whose work at FEMA has drawn scrutiny from Congress as well as the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general, was subcontracted by a company owned by Kyle Schutt, a DOGE operative whose own company was contracting with DHS.

The documents were filed in a lawsuit contesting President Donald Trump’s vast cuts to the federal workforce. Previous filings have indicated that for several months, authority over some of the spending operations of FEMA, a constituent agency of DHS, was seemingly illegally influenced by Voorhies. An April letter from three Democratic members of Congress alleges that she had outsize “power to not only influence the award of contracts and grants but also to punish entities.”

“Federal law prohibits government contractors from performing work that is characterized as ‘inherently governmental functions,’” Mississippi Democratic congressman Bennie G. Thompson wrote in the letter.

These new details from the court filings raise even further questions about DOGE members’ roles within government and the depth of possible corruption at DHS under former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem. DHS, Voorhies, and Schutt did not respond to a request for comment.

In a deposition filed as part of a lawsuit brought by the American Federation of Government Employees, Voorhies describes herself as having a “financial background” with “executive level leadership and experience.” She says she joined DHS in April 2025, coming from Crest Investment Company—a financial fund run by Jamal Daniel, an investor and founder of the Middle East–focused news outlet Al-Monitor.

According to her deposition, Voorhies was serving as chief financial officer for the company and running special projects when Daniel asked if she would be interested in working with FEMA. He introduced her to Corey Lewandowski, who at the time was a senior adviser and effectively the chief of staff for Noem. Lewandowski did not respond to a request for comment.

Voorhies, who had no previous government experience, was not paid by the government as a special government employee. SGEs are subject to fewer transparency and disclosure requirements than federal employees but are limited to working in government for 130 days per year.

Though Voorhies says she was brought in to improve “efficiency and responsiveness of FEMA,” she struggled during the deposition to define what exactly “efficiency” meant and said she was never given a formal job description. According to her deposition, Voorhies was responsible for "reviewing memos" that accompanied contracts and grant requests above $100,000 and was involved in reviewing and terminating FEMA grants. She says she did not “have authority to make decisions” at the agency, and Lewandowski and a former top aide to Noem, Joseph Guy, did not provide her with much information about FEMA.

“I recall Kyle Schutt having provided most of the information from things they had collected from DOGE,” she testified. Schutt is a software engineer who formerly served as the chief technical officer of Revv, a fundraising platform, before he joined DOGE. Schutt was, during this time period, stationed across several agencies, including the General Services Administration, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the Department of Health and Human Services, and DHS. Last year, WIRED reported that Schutt was making $195,000 as a GSA employee, and ProPublica found that Schutt was part of shuttering DHS’s Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. In May 2025 it was revealed that Schutt’s login credentials had been compromised by malware, after DropSite News reported that Schutt had been given access to FEMA’s payment software.

Voorhies testified that though she was not part of DOGE, she was working alongside the DOGE team at DHS. Part of that work involved analyzing documents that Schutt and the other DOGE FEMA members collected, such as “financial statements” and “organizational charts.” After her time as an SGE ran out in the fall of 2025, though, she spoke to Schutt and Lewandowski about how she could continue working with DHS, she said. The solution, as she explained in her deposition: Voorhies would be brought on as a subcontractor to another subcontractor, owned by Schutt.

In her deposition, Voorhies said that in September 2025, she started LV Consulting, a company where she was the only employee. In October, this company began serving as a subcontractor to AnchorCode Technologies, which was owned by Schutt and was itself already serving as a subcontractor to another company, IMGE.

IMGE was the “prime” contractor—the company with the direct contract with DHS. As subcontractors, AnchorCode and LV Consulting did not have direct contracts with DHS and do not appear in the System for Award Management, the system that shows which companies contract with the government.

AnchorCode did not respond to a request for comment.

IMGE describes itself as a “full-service” marketing agency that offers “audience intelligence, advanced advertising, AI-powered analytics, influencer marketing, advocacy toolsets, and always-on testing.” It appears to be a subsidiary of a much larger communications agency called GP3 Partners and has worked with US Senator Rand Paul’s campaign and Advancing American Freedom, a conservative advocacy organization founded by former vice president Mike Pence.

IMGE and GP3 did not respond to a request for comment.

A federal employee with expertise in the government’s contracting system, who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the press, tells WIRED that the overlying companies and their various government contracts seem to be highly suspect.

“If you’re a senior adviser to an agency and that agency is giving you contracts or subcontracts, that’s a huge no-no,” says the federal employee. “This is literally the reason ethics rules even exist.”

Schutt’s employment at GSA, the employee says, raises additional concerns. “An important ethics question would also be whether he became privy to procurement-sensitive data while he was a federal employee at DHS, which is highly likely if he was at GSA, because the main thing they do is acquisition and procurement,” they say.

In order to keep this kind of deal aboveboard, the federal employee says, Schutt and Voorhies would have needed to go to the agency’s ethics officer as well as to the Office of Government Ethics to ensure there was no conflict of interest. For someone who was a government employee, as Schutt appeared to be at GSA, the federal employee says, there would normally need to be a “cooling-off period” between a person’s government tenure and their contracting work.

Margaret Dylus-Yukins, senior legal counsel for ethics at the Campaign Legal Center and a former attorney adviser to the Office of Government Ethics, tells WIRED that Voorhies was seemingly powerful enough within FEMA that she would likely have been subject to a two-year ban on communicating with the agency after ending her time as an SGE, unless she had been granted a special waiver. (WIRED was not able to find a waiver for Voorhies or Schutt on the Federal Register.) Based on her understanding of Voorhies’ situation, Dylus-Yukins alleges, "this is illegal under 18 USD 207 of the criminal code.”

Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, says that if there is an appearance of a conflict of interest, other contractors could sue IMGE, alleging that in subcontracting to Schutt and Voorhies, the company had an unfair advantage.

Tillipman notes that if someone sets up a company to contract with an agency while still a government employee, that could be a violation of the law. AnchorCode was founded in 2023 but registered on the System for Award Management in October 2025. But even so, it could still be an ethics concern. “Some of this is still murky, but at its core, at minimum, there does seem to be an appearance issue. And it raises red flags.”

It is not clear from Voorhies’ deposition when AnchorCode’s contract with IMGE began, but Voorhies says that her contract with AnchorCode ran from October 1, 2025, until mid-March 2026, when it was terminated a week after Trump announced that he would be replacing Noem as Homeland Security secretary.

AnchorCode’s website does not list any team members and describes the company as building “mission-specific software for government.” In her deposition, when asked about Schutt, Voorhies says that “he was AnchorCode.” For her work as a contractor with AnchorCode, Voorhies testified that she was paid $325 an hour and said that she did not have to go through any sort of public bidding process in order to win it.

Both Schutt and Voorhies retained their titles as senior advisers, even though they were contractors, and Voorhies says in her deposition that she never informed her colleagues at DHS that her position had effectively changed.

Schutt is not the only DOGE member who appears to have used their time in government to possibly access government contracts. In May, WIRED reported that former DOGE member Ethan Shaotran, one of the young engineers who comprised some of the group’s core members, was starting a defense tech startup positioning itself to receive government contracts.

Tillipman says that these hiring situations involving the private sector, DOGE, the Trump administration, and SGEs undermine trust in the government.

“When you have a huge number of special government employees that are also maintaining outside business interests with organizations or entities or firms that continue to do business with the government, it raises those optics concerns,” she says.

The Trump administration has repeatedly indicated that it wants to eliminate FEMA, and last week, 25 Democratic-led states filed a lawsuit alleging that FEMA’s disaster aid had been cut to their states in retaliation in order to force them to use the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services’ SAVE database to check their voter rolls against DHS’s immigration records.

entries.title: Big Tech Wants to Harvest Your Thoughts
entries.summary: Silicon Valley companies are already working on neurotechnology products that track your brain activity. The next privacy frontier might be the things you only think.
entries.content:
Rafael Yuste is in his early sixties and bears a more than passing resemblance to Pablo Picasso—if Picasso had worn glasses and had a trim white goatee. Speaking succinctly and methodically, his accent rich with Spanish inflections, he told me about an experiment he had carried out in his lab at Columbia on the brains of mice, and specifically on that part of the cortex that responds to vision. His mentor had been the Swedish neuroscientist Torsten Wiesel, who won a Nobel Prize for his research into how our visual systems process information.

“He discovered by chance that the strongest stimulus is a pattern of high-contrast dark and light bars.” He held up one hand and waved his fingers back and forth. “If you imagine my fingers were bars of light surrounded by complete blackness—if I move my fingers in front of your eyes, that fires up your whole visual cortex.”

To begin with, they used these moving images to train the mice. The bars were projected onto a computer screen in front of them, and when they moved up and down, it was a cue to take a drink from a tube of water. When they moved from side to side, they were to stop drinking.
